agent2_stories.headline: Council approves on-bill financing for efficiency upgrades
agent2_stories.draft:
Longmont's city council gave final approval to an on-bill financing program that lets property owners repay the cost of efficiency work through the utility bill rather than in one payment. The ordinance covers insulation, air sealing, heat pumps, and the electrical work those upgrades require, and it applies to owners and, with the owner's consent, to renters.

The program's administrator is Longmont Power & Communications, which already bills most addresses in the city. Participants sign a repayment agreement that follows the meter: the balance transfers with the property if it is sold, and the city has said participation is voluntary and tied to a credit check. The council set the interest rate in the ordinance rather than leaving it to staff.

Staff told the council the program responds to owners who want to cut energy use but cannot carry the full cost in one season. The council asked for a report after the first year covering how many projects were completed, in which neighborhoods, and how many applicants were turned down. The program begins after the ordinance is published; owners should wait for the city's own application page before signing anything with a contractor.
agent2_stories.plainLanguage: The city council approved a program that lets owners pay for insulation, heat pumps, and related electrical work a little at a time on their utility bill. It is voluntary, and the city says the debt follows the property if it is sold. The city has not published the application page yet.

agent2_stories.headline: Students to prepare free evening meals for Longmont seniors
agent2_stories.draft:
Longmont's Senior Center plans to begin offering free take-home evening meals on Friday, Oct. 2, through a partnership with St. Vrain Valley Schools' ProStart and Culinary Arts program. Students at the district's Career Elevation and Technology Center will make chilled dinners designed with seniors' dietary needs in mind, according to the city's Sept. 24 announcement. The same school program will also provide meals for young people in city Children, Youth and Families programming.

Meals will be available at 3 p.m. on select dates at the Senior Center, 910 Longs Peak Avenue. The city lists Fridays Oct. 2, 16 and 30; Nov. 13; and Dec. 11, plus Tuesdays Nov. 24 and Dec. 22. Residents can call Senior Services at 303-651-8411 for current details before making a trip.

Senior Services Manager Ronnie Maynes says funding currently runs through the end of 2026 and the city is exploring ways to continue in 2027.
agent2_stories.plainLanguage: Beginning Oct. 2, the Longmont Senior Center says it will give out free evening meals for people to take home. Students in a St. Vrain Valley Schools culinary program will prepare the chilled dinners.

agent3_blackDesk.source: Tier B secondary report on the Sept. 22 council meeting
agent3_blackDesk.title: The Dry Creek annexation may have been amended to shrink the bike-share condition
agent3_blackDesk.speculativeAngle: The hypothesis is that the ordinance the council actually advanced is not the ordinance in the cached agenda, and that the difference sits in the bike-share and traffic-condition language rather than in the annexation itself. A change of that kind would be invisible to anyone reading the agenda alone, and it would matter to the residents on the affected streets, who were told at the first reading what the conditions were. This run could not confirm any part of it: the original PrimeGov packet timed out, the video captions came back empty, and no posted minutes were located, so the only account of an amendment is a Tier B secondary report that could not be checked against a record. Nothing here establishes that an amendment happened, what it said, or who moved it.
agent3_blackDesk.investigationQuestion: Did the ordinance the council advanced on Sept. 22 differ from the ordinance in the cached agenda, and if so, what exactly changed between the two texts?
agent3_blackDesk.vulnerabilityDetail: The only account of the amendment is a secondary report; the primary record was not read at all.
agent3_blackDesk.agent4Target: Compare the cached ordinance text with the posted minutes and the Oct. 6 second reading.

agent3_blackDesk.title: The police and fire union agreements may set a pay pattern the 2027 budget cannot hold
agent3_blackDesk.speculativeAngle: The hypothesis is that the two 2027-28 union agreements, taken together, set a compensation pattern across the two largest departments that the 2027 proposed budget does not fund at the level the agreements imply, and that the gap would surface later as either a mid-year appropriation or a service reduction rather than as a tax question put to voters. It is a hypothesis and nothing more: this run has not read the agreements' salary schedules, has not matched them to a budget line, and does not know whether the council approved them, amended them, or continued them. The reason to write it down anyway is that the same council received a 2027 budget presentation the same evening, in the same meeting, and no account this run read connects the two.
agent3_blackDesk.investigationQuestion: Do the police and fire agreements' salary schedules fit inside the 2027 proposed budget's public-safety line, or do they imply a gap?
agent3_blackDesk.vulnerabilityDetail: Neither the resolutions nor the budget document were read.
agent3_blackDesk.agent4Target: Read both resolutions and match their schedules to the 2027 proposed budget.
